figures.caption: Table 1: Target signatures used to evaluate candidate stress perturbations.

Figure 2: Stress training preserves task performance under stress but introduces a delay-generalisation trade-off. (a) Psychometric accuracy as a function of stimulus evidence, |∆| = |S2 − S1|, for naïve (blue) and resilient (orange) networks. Left: without test-time stress, the two classes are nearly identical across evidence levels, confirming that stress training leaves baseline performance intact. Right: under S↑[WI→E ] stress at δ = 0.25, resilient networks maintain substantially higher accuracy than naïve networks, most markedly at intermediate evidence. (b) Delay-task accuracy as a function of memory delay. Left: without test-time stress, both classes perform similarly within the trained delay range but resilient networks degrade faster at long, out-of-distribution delays. Right: under the same stress, naïve accuracy falls to the resilient out-of-distribution level, so the two classes converge at long delays while resilient networks retain their advantage only within the trained range. Blue shaded regions mark the stimulus-evidence (a) or delay (b) ranges used during training; unshaded regions correspond to out-of-distribution generalisation tests. Curves show the mean over 50 independently trained networks per class, and shaded bands indicate the SEM.

Figure 3: Stress-induced changes in task performance and network dynamics. Each cell shows the signed percentage change relative to the unperturbed baseline (δ = 0, σstress = 0; Eq. 11), with diagonally split cells: upper-left triangle at δT = 0.5 (within training range) and lower-right triangle at δmax = 1.0 (beyond training range). Rows are grouped into biologically targeted protocols and population-agnostic controls (separated by a dashed line). Orange/blue indicates increase/decrease; colour saturates at ±100%, and values exceeding this range are annotated as > 100%. (a) Performance metrics (accuracy, MSE, and decision confidence) for Naive (left) and Resilient (right) networks. (b) Internal dynamics (population firing rates r̄E , r̄I ; absolute synaptic drive components hE→E , |hI→E |, hE→I , |hI→I |; and excitatory-to-inhibitory drive ratio E/|I|) for Naive (left) and Resilient (right) networks. The highlighted row (S↑[WI→E ]) corresponds to the mechanism that best reproduces the target stress signatures.

Figure 4: Stress resilience produces a context-dependent delay-generalisation trade-off. The figure is a 2 × 2 array of blocks. Top blocks (a, b) report raw accuracy; bottom blocks (c, d) report the naïve-minus-resilient difference ∆a = aNaive − aResilient. Left blocks (a, c) use within-distribution delays (400–900 ms, the trained range); right blocks (b, d) use long out-of-distribution delays (OOD-high, > 900 ms). Within every block, the two sub-panels sweep a different training variable: sub-panel A varies the training stress magnitude δT , and sub-panel B varies the recurrent network size N . (a, b) Accuracy for naïve (blue) and resilient (orange) networks, each evaluated without test-time stress (solid lines) and under acute stress at δ = 0.25 (dashed lines). The grey dashed line marks chance (0.5). (c, d) The group difference ∆a evaluated without stress (blue) and under acute stress at δ = 0.25 (orange); here colour encodes the evaluation condition rather than network type. Positive ∆a indicates better naïve performance and negative ∆a better resilient performance, and the grey dashed line marks no difference (∆a = 0). Each point is the mean over 50 independently trained networks per class, and shaded bands show the SEM.

Figure 5: Stress training preserves recurrent population geometry and constrains energetic collapse under perturbation. Naïve networks (blue) and stress-trained resilient networks (orange) were analysed under inhibitoryto-excitatory weight perturbations, S↑[WI→E ], of strength δ. (a) Representative PCA projections of recurrent rate trajectories for a matched seed pair, shown in the top three baseline PCs. Solid lines show unstressed baseline trajectories for two choice directions at the largest tested |∆|; dashed and dotted lines show the corresponding stressed trajectories at δ = 0.25 and δ = 0.5. Naïve trajectories are strongly displaced under stress, whereas resilient trajectories remain closer to the baseline dynamical manifold. (b) Mean Euclidean displacement of stressed trajectories from their corresponding baseline trajectories, computed in the top-k baseline PCA subspace explaining 90% of baseline variance. (c) Fraction of stressed activity variance retained within the same top-k baseline subspace. The dashed line marks the 90% baselinevariance reference used to define the subspace. (d) Mean per-timestep metabolic energy, E(t) = α1R+ α2(SE + SI), decomposed into activity cost R, excitatory-target synaptic cost SE , and inhibitory-target synaptic cost SI . Naïve networks show a large stress-induced reduction in total energy, whereas resilient networks maintain energy closer to baseline.

Figure 6: Stress resilience is associated with a reorganization of recurrent network topology. Density (a) and weighted directed reciprocity (b) for trained recurrent connectivity matrices. Each point represents one trained network (n = 200 networks per condition). Black circles indicate group means ± SEM. Statistical comparisons use two-sided Mann–Whitney U tests, with *** indicating p < 0.001.

Table 2: Full statistics for the delay-generalisation trade-off analysis. Mean accuracies are reported for Naive versus Resilient networks; ∆ = aNaive − aResilient (positive favours Naive). Group comparisons are Welch t-tests; all were confirmed with HC3-robust OLS (HC3 p within an order of magnitude of the Welch p in every row; e.g. p = 0.540, < 10−300, 9.1× 10−25, 0.0037, 0.053, 4.8× 10−160, 1.3× 10−21, and 0.110 for the rows above, top to bottom). The interaction column reports the group-by-covariate term (δmax for the stress-magnitude sweep, N for the network-size sweep); a significant interaction indicates that the Naive–Resilient gap changed across the swept variable.

Table 3: Full statistics for the recurrent dynamics and geometry analysis. Values give the compared quantities (Naive vs. Resilient for cross-group rows; δ = 0.25 vs. δ = 0.5 for within-group rows). MWU, Mann–Whitney U test; BF, Brown–Forsythe test (variance). For energy-deviation variance, values are standard deviations across seeds.
